title: Compile a transfer: the rowcount is the guard
objective: Write a compile plan for Transfer(from, to, amount) in which every UPDATE expects exactly one row, every zero maps to a named outcome (Insufficient, NoSuchAccount(from), NoSuchAccount(to)), the schema says NOT NULL CHECK (bal >= 0), and a self-transfer follows your decision record; then find the witnesses that break mutant plans.

blocks.md: A transfer is two UPDATEs. In your model each step either happens or the command is refused with a reason. In SQL an UPDATE that matches no row succeeds and changes nothing, and the row count is the only place the database says so. If typed error outcomes are new to you, drawer D-23 is one page on them.

choice.prompt: Your debit `UPDATE acct SET bal = bal - $2 WHERE id = $1 AND bal >= $2` reports 0 rows on a table where `bal` may be NULL. What could have happened?

options.text: Only insufficient funds; the other causes raise errors.
options.why: Three other causes give the same zero, and none of them raises an error.

options.text: A serialization failure from a concurrent writer.
options.why: A serialization failure raises an error. It never returns 0 rows.

options.text: Any of four: low funds, a missing account, a NULL balance, a NULL amount.
options.why: All four returned 0 rows with no error in the recorded run {{run:RUN-pg-claims}}.

options.text: Nothing: an UPDATE that matches no row raises an error.
options.why: Matching no row is a success with a count of 0.

choice.prompt: Now declare `bal NOT NULL`. Which causes of a 0-row debit remain?

options.text: Three: all but the NULL balance.
options.why: `NOT NULL` constrains stored rows. It does not constrain parameters or missing rows {{run:RUN-pg-claims}}.

options.text: All four.
options.why: A NULL balance can no longer be stored.

options.text: Two: low funds and a missing account.
options.why: A NULL amount still makes the guard unknown, so it still selects nothing.

options.text: Only low funds.
options.why: A missing account still matches nothing.

segments.title: Why a debit reports zero rows

blocks.md: Run five statements on a table where `bal` may be NULL: four debits that fail in four different ways, then a credit to an account that does not exist.
Account 1 holds 100 and account 2 holds NULL.
blocks.direction: Read the row count each UPDATE reports, and whether any statement raises an error.

call.prompt: `UPDATE acct SET bal = bal + 30 WHERE id = 999`, and no row 999 exists. PostgreSQL returns:

options.text: A new row 999 with balance 30.
options.why: UPDATE never inserts.

options.text: Success, 1 row.
options.why: No row matches, so no row is counted.

options.text: An error naming the missing row.
options.why: SQL reports a count, not a missing key.

options.text: Success, 0 rows.
options.why: The statement succeeds and changes nothing.

blocks.after: All four debits and the credit reported the same thing: zero rows, no error {{run:RUN-pg-claims}}. If your plan ignores the credit's zero, the debit commits and 30 leaves the system.

blocks.md:
A plan that cannot miss a zero declares how many rows each UPDATE expects and turns every zero into a named outcome inside the transaction. Here is the reference plan. Read it once before the witness question.

```text
schema  acct(id int PRIMARY KEY, bal bigint NOT NULL CHECK (bal >= 0))
plan Transfer(from, to, amt)          -- amt > 0 by type
  if from = to and your decision rejects it: Err SelfTransfer   -- before any SQL
  BEGIN
  s1  UPDATE acct SET bal = bal - $amt WHERE id = $from AND bal >= $amt
      RETURNING old.bal, new.bal      -- expect exactly 1 row
      0 rows: SELECT 1 FROM acct WHERE id = $from
              none -> Err NoSuchAccount(from); some -> Err Insufficient; ROLLBACK
  s2  UPDATE acct SET bal = bal + $amt WHERE id = $to
      RETURNING old.bal, new.bal      -- expect exactly 1 row
      0 rows -> Err NoSuchAccount(to); ROLLBACK
  SQLSTATE 22003 -> the decision of S6.L4; ROLLBACK
  COMMIT -> Ok(the two old/new pairs)
```

`RETURNING old.bal, new.bal` is new in PostgreSQL 18 {{run:RUN-pg-sql-semantics}}. Each pair is one row's concrete step from D to D′, which S6.L8 uses. Expectations are equalities, never "at least one". If your decision allows a self-transfer, the two UPDATEs handle it: the guard still runs, so one above the balance is refused as `Insufficient`.

choice.prompt: A plan matches the reference except in one place: its credit declares no expectation, so a credit that updates zero rows goes unnoticed. Which initial state and command make its outcome differ from the reference's?

options.text: Account 1 holds 100 and account 2 does not exist; transfer 30 from 1 to 2.
options.why: The debit commits, the credit updates no row, and the plan returns success. The reference refuses with `NoSuchAccount(to)` and rolls back.

options.text: Accounts 1 and 2 hold 100 each; transfer 30 from 1 to 2.
options.why: Both plans commit the same two changes.

options.text: Account 1 holds 20; transfer 30 from 1 to 2.
options.why: The debit's guard fails in both plans, so both refuse with `Insufficient` and the credit never runs.

options.text: Account 1 does not exist; transfer 30 from 1 to 2.
options.why: The debit's own expectation catches a missing `from` in both plans.

segments.title: The schema is part of the compile

blocks.md: Look at the schema line of the plan: `NOT NULL CHECK (bal >= 0)`. It is part of the compile. Without `NOT NULL` a NULL balance can be stored and the guard skips it. With `NOT NULL` that cause is gone, but a NULL amount and a missing account still give zero rows. A second question: if the schema keeps the `CHECK`, does the plan still need its guard?
The debit has no guard. The schema keeps `CHECK (bal >= 0)`.
blocks.direction: Debit 80 from a balance of 50 with no guard in the statement. Read what the UPDATE reports and what the SELECT shows.

call.prompt: No guard; the schema keeps `CHECK (bal >= 0)`. Debit 80 from a balance of 50. PostgreSQL:

options.text: Commits, leaving a balance of -30.
options.why: A false result is rejected. Only NULL slips through.

options.text: Fails with a check violation.
options.why: The new row would make the constraint false, so the statement errors.

options.text: Skips the row and updates 0 rows.
options.why: A constraint does not filter rows the way WHERE does.

options.text: Commits, clamping the balance at 0.
options.why: Nothing clamps. The database refuses or stores the value.

blocks.after: The balance is unchanged, the same as after a guarded refusal. The outcome is not the same: your semantics says `Insufficient`, and the database raises a check violation (SQLSTATE 23514 {{run:RUN-pg-sql-semantics}}). A harness that compares final balances alone calls the two equal.

options.text: With `CHECK` alone, an overdraft's outcome equals the semantics' `Insufficient`.
options.why: The database raises a check violation, a different outcome class.

options.text: A debit that updates 0 rows says which account was missing.
options.why: Zero rows says only that nothing matched. One more query tells low funds from a missing account.

options.text: `RETURNING old.bal, new.bal` still returns a row when the guard matches nothing.
options.why: `RETURNING` reports updated rows only, so zero updated rows returns nothing.

options.text: With `NOT NULL` and the guard, a NULL amount still yields 0 rows.
options.why: `bal >= NULL` is unknown, so the guard selects nothing and no write happens {{run:RUN-pg-claims}}.

blocks.md: S2's self-transfer bug (SP-2.1) comes back in SQL. Your decision record from LAB-3.7 says what a self-transfer means, and the compiler has to act on it. If you have not recorded that decision yet, use the reference's: a self-transfer is allowed and changes nothing. Here is the compile that saves a round trip: one statement with a CASE, then the two-UPDATE version.
Account 1 holds 100. The command moves 30 from account 1 to account 1.
blocks.direction: The first UPDATE is the one-statement plan with `$from`, `$to` and `$amt` filled in. Compare the two SELECTs.

call.prompt: One statement: `SET bal = CASE WHEN id = $from THEN bal - $amt WHEN id = $to THEN bal + $amt END WHERE id IN ($from, $to)`, with from = to = 1 and amount 30. Afterwards:

options.text: Balance 100, 2 rows updated.
options.why: One row matches, and only the first true CASE arm applies.

options.text: An error: one row updated twice.
options.why: The single matching row is updated once, and nothing reports the overlap.

options.text: Balance 70, 1 row updated.
options.why: The debit arm wins and 30 disappears. The two-UPDATE plan leaves 100.

options.text: Balance 130, 1 row updated.
options.why: CASE takes the first true arm, not the last.

blocks.after: The one-statement plan ended at 70, and the two-UPDATE plan ended at 100.

blocks.md: The compile assumed `from` and `to` are different accounts. With exact expectations the CASE plan would have expected two rows, received one and rolled back, so the rowcount check catches it. Without them it commits and destroys 30.

choice.prompt: A one-statement CASE plan and the two-UPDATE plan both keep `NOT NULL CHECK (bal >= 0)`, and neither checks a rowcount. They give the same outcome on every command except one kind. Which kind?

options.text: A transfer larger than the sender's balance.
options.why: Both plans raise the same check violation.

options.text: A transfer from an account to itself.
options.why: The CASE plan applies only the debit arm, and the two-UPDATE plan leaves the balance unchanged.

options.text: A transfer to an account that does not exist.
options.why: Both plans debit the sender and credit nothing.

options.text: A transfer whose amount is NULL.
options.why: Both plans fail on the NOT NULL constraint.

choice.prompt: Which statement about compiling Transfer is true?

options.text: With a declared expectation of exactly one row, a missing `to` account is caught before COMMIT.
options.why: The credit reports zero rows, the plan sees it, and the transaction rolls back.

options.text: A debit that matches no row raises an error, so the plan needs no rowcount check.
options.why: Matching no row is a success with a count of 0.

options.text: A self-transfer compiled as one CASE statement leaves the balance as the two-UPDATE plan does.
options.why: The CASE plan applies only its first true arm and loses the amount.

options.text: Keeping the `CHECK` makes the guard in the debit redundant.
options.why: Without the guard the outcome is a check violation, not `Insufficient`.

choice.prompt: A plan differs from the reference only in its guard: `bal > $amt` where the reference has `bal >= $amt`. Which command separates them?

options.text: Debit 30 from a balance of 100.
options.why: Both guards pass and both plans commit.

options.text: Debit 130 from a balance of 100.
options.why: Both guards fail, and both plans report `Insufficient`.

options.text: Debit 100 from a balance of 100.
options.why: The reference commits and leaves 0. The strict guard matches no row, and the plan reports `Insufficient`.

options.text: Debit 30 from an account that does not exist.
options.why: Both plans find the account missing and report `NoSuchAccount(from)`.

blocks.title: Production twin: TigerBeetle
blocks.md: TigerBeetle's `create_transfers` names every refusal as a result code, among them `accounts_must_be_different`, `debit_account_not_found` and `exceeds_credits` (https://docs.tigerbeetle.com/reference/requests/create_transfers/, read 2026-10-23; pins in {{run:RUN-twin-pins}}). Map your typed outcomes to its results. Which of your zero-row causes can its interface not produce?
